A1.justification: Both PDFs describe D2NWG, with the same core framework and identifiable retained experiments. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original weight-generation and fine-tuning experiments on vision datasets, including KaggleZoo, MobileNet transfer and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original vision results and reports additional few-shot, architecture-transfer, GLUE and language-model experiments in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The VAE, dataset encoder and latent-diffusion core remain. v2 adds layer-wise chunking, chunk-index conditioning, language-task-description encoding, spectral layer selection and validation-guided sequential weight replacement for LLMs (Sections 3.2–3.5, Appendix A.3–A.4 and Algorithm 1). These substantially extend the generation and inference procedures.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained vision coverage, v2 evaluates mini-ImageNet and tiered-ImageNet few-shot tasks, 30 Meta-Album datasets, Aircraft, Pets and CIFAR-100. It also introduces six GLUE tasks and language-model reasoning, instruction-following and knowledge benchmarks, substantially expanding the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated GHN2/GHN3, SANE variants, pdiff, meta-learning methods including MetaDiff, and LoRA/AdaLoRA/DyLoRA/FourierFT comparisons. Within the ConvNet fine-tuning comparison, Table 4 introduces RandomInit and SANE alongside SKDE30, while the pretrained-continuation comparator from v1 Tables 1 and 6 is absent from that table.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50,000-task few-shot training collections, 600 evaluation tasks, averaging the top three of 50 sampled heads, and LLM validation-based selection and benchmark-specific shot settings. The existing MobileNet zoo training budget is also reported differently: 25 epochs in v1 Section 4.3 versus 15 in v2 Appendix C.11. This documents a setting revision without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v2 retains the model-zoo-size, latent-space, encoder and predictor analyses, largely relocating them. It adds mixed-architecture and unseen-architecture tests, full-model versus classifier-head comparisons, sampled-weight distribution visualizations and qualitative language-generation cases (Appendix C, Figure 10 and Tables 12 and 22). These investigate substantial additional capability and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: The revised MobileNet comparison reports uncertainty terms in v2 Table 22, whereas v1 Table 4 gives point estimates. The three-run KaggleZoo reporting already present in v1 Table 9 remains in v2 Table 21. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated-run or seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results and replaces the main ConvNet and MobileNet comparisons under revised settings. New results include Meta-Album average accuracy of 69.47 versus 68.32 for pretrained models (Table 3), and GPT-2 leaderboard averages of 6.29 versus 6.30 (Table 17). Earlier cross-dataset, predictor, encoder and Kaggle tables are numerically retained as Tables 18–21.

T1.justification: The original gradient-descent argument and principal contrastive and diffusion equations remain. Appendix A.3 adds a localized mathematical treatment of Marchenko–Pastur spectral bounds and a signal-to-noise definition supporting layer selection. No new theorem or proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims effective dataset-conditioned initialization and faster transfer on vision tasks. v2 additionally claims superiority to meta-learning methods, generation approaching a billion parameters, and improved LLM weights from a single pretrained model without direct fine-tuning. These substantially broaden the abstract, contribution list and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds shared-manifold and spectral-signal explanations for LLM weight search, interpretations of model retrieval and full-model generation, and storage and weight-symmetry limitations. It removes v1's explanation connecting Dessert performance to similar training images and its qualification about target datasets exceeding training class counts, changing important applicability guidance.

D1.justification: v2 documents exact LLM chunk sizes, layer grouping, selection pseudocode, task descriptions, Meta-Album preparation and model-component parameter counts. Much of the original optimizer configuration remains. The promised GitHub code-release statement disappears, while links to generated Llama models are added; these are changes in documented access information.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially to recent scalable weight-generation methods, few-shot meta-learning, LoRA retrieval and adaptation, and LLMs. New discussions of Wang et al. (2024), Schürholt et al. (2024), MetaDiff and Spectrum help position D2NWG around scalability and cross-domain generation beyond v1's primarily vision-transfer framing.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, existing methodological explanations are revised, and experiments are reorganized around generation without fine-tuning, transfer and language-model applications. Original ablations move into reorganized appendices, with substantial changes to headings and narrative structure beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column presentation, redraws the framework diagram, adds a dataset-encoder diagram and new experimental displays, and restructures comparison tables. Earlier convergence panels are selectively combined in Figure 2, while original convergence and ablation figures are relocated to the appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for scalability and comparison with competing methods, which were limited in v1. Explicit chunking and layer-selection procedures, unseen-architecture tests, LLM evaluations, and comparisons with GHN, SANE, pdiff and meta-learning methods make the contribution substantially better supported. These gains outweigh the loss of useful dataset-similarity and class-count qualifications, although unclear top-k selection details and overly broad performance language still limit some new claims.
